---
title: "EmpiricalCalibration"
subtitle: "Calibrating p-values and confidence intervals against what a study actually gets wrong"
toc: false
---

Observational studies of healthcare data produce effect estimates with
confidence intervals and p-values computed as though **random error were the
only error**. It is not. Confounding, selection bias and measurement error add a
*systematic* component that the standard error does not know about, and the
result is inference that is far more confident than it deserves to be.

Empirical calibration measures that systematic component instead of assuming it
away. Run your study design on a set of **negative controls** — exposure–outcome
pairs where the true effect is known to be null — and the spread of the
estimates you get back is a direct, empirical picture of your study's error. The
distribution fitted to those estimates is the *empirical null*, and p-values and
confidence intervals evaluated against it carry the study's real uncertainty
rather than its nominal one.

::: {.keyresult}
Traditional p-value: how surprising is this estimate **if the null is true and
the study is unbiased**?

Calibrated p-value: how surprising is this estimate **if the null is true and
the study is as biased as it demonstrably is on things we know are null**?
:::

## Install

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/ablack3/EmpyriCal.git
```

## Sixty seconds

```{python}
import empiricalcalibration as ec

sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]
positive = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 1]

null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
print(null)
```

The negative controls should have been centred on a log relative risk of 0 with
no spread beyond their own standard errors. They are centred on 0.79 — a
relative risk of `{python} round(float(__import__("numpy").exp(null[0])), 2)` —
with a further 0.28 of standard deviation on top. That is this study design's
systematic error, and every estimate it produces inherits it.

```{python}
print("traditional p:", ec.computeTraditionalP(positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr)[0])
print("calibrated  p:", ec.calibrateP(null, positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr)[0])
```

The positive control — a drug–outcome pair with a *known* effect — goes from
"certain" to "unremarkable". Read that as a statement about the study design,
not about the drug: a design that finds this much signal in outcomes it should
find nothing in cannot support a confident claim here either.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Blue dots are negative controls, the yellow diamond is the positive control. The grey dashed boundary encloses results the traditional test calls significant; the orange region is what the calibrated test calls significant. Negative controls inside either region are false positives."
fig = ec.plotCalibrationEffect(
    negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr,
    positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr,
)
```

## Provenance

This package is a Python port of the OHDSI R package
[EmpiricalCalibration](https://github.com/OHDSI/EmpiricalCalibration) v3.1.4 by
Martijn Schuemie and Marc Suchard. Function names, arguments and defaults are
unchanged, and the numerical results are verified against R — see
[Validation](validation.qmd). The methods are those of @schuemie2014 and
@schuemie2018.
